title: The saturation is fine
objective: Recognize opioid-induced respiratory depression with sedation scales and capnography before the oxygen saturation falls
secondaryObjectives: Administer medications and monitor for the expected and adverse response

brief.situation: 03:40 on a progressive care unit. You are Mr. Ruiz's nurse. He is 58, the evening after a hip replacement, with obstructive sleep apnea; his home CPAP is in the room but not on. The capnography alarm sounds for the third time this hour; the aide says 'his sats are 96, it's just the sensor'.
handover: On 2 L/min oxygen by nasal cannula with continuous SpO2 and end-tidal CO2 monitoring.

IV hydromorphone as needed for pain, last given at 02:50. The unit's opioid protocol: assess sedation with the POSS before every dose; at POSS 3 or more hold opioids, stay with him and call the rapid response team; naloxone in small titrated IV doses by protocol for POSS 4 or a respiratory rate under 8.
Rapid response comes within minutes of a call.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Each assessment takes the time on its button. Decide what the numbers on the monitor mean and act on them.
Partway through you are asked to write what you think is happening. A debrief scores what you did.

why.question: His saturation is 96%. Is the capnography alarm a false alarm?

parts.label: What the numbers mean
parts.criteria: Rising end-tidal CO2 (above 55) with a slow rate, pauses and POSS 3-4 is opioid-induced respiratory depression; supplemental oxygen keeps the SpO2 normal while CO2 climbs, so the saturation is a late sign; sleep apnea adds risk.
parts.modelAnswer: No. His end-tidal CO2 has climbed past 55 with a rate of 8 and pauses, and he drifts off mid-sentence: that is opioid-induced respiratory depression. The oxygen is holding his saturation up while CO2 builds, so SpO2 will fall late. His sleep apnea makes it worse.

parts.label: What I do
parts.criteria: Hold opioids; wake him, head up, his CPAP; naloxone in small titrated doses (not a full bolus) by protocol; rapid response now; watch for resedation; no as-needed opioid.
parts.modelAnswer: Hold every opioid, wake him, head up and his CPAP on, small titrated naloxone doses by protocol, and rapid response now. No hydromorphone when he wakes in pain, and watch him for resedation as the naloxone wears off.

expertPath.text: Don't trust the saturation alone: read the capnography trend and count his breathing. EtCO2 56 and rising, rate 8 with pauses.
Wake him: POSS 3. Hold all opioids. Head up, his CPAP on.
Rapid response now; naloxone in small titrated doses by protocol.
SBAR; watch for resedation; no as-needed hydromorphone.

reversal.headline: Abrupt reversal
reversal.body: Naloxone in postoperative opioid depression is titrated in small doses to breathing. A full bolus can cause severe pain, hypertension, arrhythmias and pulmonary edema.

apnea.headline: Apnea
apnea.body: On oxygen, the saturation stays normal while CO2 climbs. Rising end-tidal CO2 with sedation is the early warning; silence it and you lose it.

rescued.headline: Caught early
rescued.body: You read the capnography over the saturation, scored his sedation, held opioids, put his CPAP on, titrated naloxone and called rapid response. That is the expert path.

rescuedLate.headline: Rescued, with gaps
rescuedLate.body: Check the time to the call, whether the alarm was silenced, whether his CPAP went on, and whether he had more opioid.

time_up.headline: Unescalated
time_up.body: POSS 3 or rising CO2 means a call within minutes.

scoring.modelReasoning: A rising end-tidal CO2 above 55, a respiratory rate of 8 with pauses and a POSS of 3-4 is opioid-induced respiratory depression, even with an SpO2 of 96%: supplemental oxygen keeps the saturation normal while CO2 builds, and sleep apnea adds to it. Hold all opioids, wake him, head up and CPAP on, naloxone in small titrated doses by protocol, rapid response now, and watch for resedation because naloxone can wear off before the opioid. No as-needed hydromorphone, and the alarm stays on.

spo2Q.ask: While you assess: why can his saturation look fine while his breathing fails?

choices.label: Supplemental oxygen keeps the SpO2 up while CO2 builds; capnography shows the CO2
If the SpO2 is normal, his breathing is adequate

spo2Q.explain: Patients on PCA with hypercarbia were sedated while their SpO2 values remained normal; end-tidal values above 55 marked significant respiratory depression.
